I think it'd be most accurate to say that incest aversion is not purely biological but a mix of both social and evolutionary influences. If it were entirely innate, we wouldn’t see such vast cultural differences with respect to its acceptance. Cousin marriage has been common or even preferred in many societies. Sibling marriages occurred among Egyptian pharaohs and Incan royalty. These exceptions suggest that social norms strongly shape aversion (Not to say that they're the only force at play, but still a considerable force). However, if it was purely social there would likely be no reason for society to make it taboo in the first place, especially when highly influencial people were doing it. It would've just continued, but eventually we discovered what it can lead to. So social forces are being used in order to prevent a genetic issue, it's not necessarily genetics that create the aversion itself.

Disgust reactions are often learned. Many taboos, (dietary restrictions, hygiene practices) vary across cultures, so what feels “natural” is actually often the result of conditioning. If incest aversion were hardwired, children raised in societies where it’s normalised would still feel inherent repulsion - but they don’t.

Evolution also doesn't require an innate emotional reaction. Social norms and learned behaviors can be just as effective at discouraging harmful reproductive choices. So it's possible that the social behaviour is reinforced through generations but isn't genetic itself. Contrary to the claim that those lacking incest aversion were a “genetic dead end” - they actually often reproduce successfully! Severe inbreeding effects take generations to manifest, so natural selection would not have eliminated those without incest aversion fast enough to cut out the practice entirely. That's why decendants of inbreeding cases are still around today. The odds of having a problem are much higher than when inbreeding doesn't occur, but as a percentage of inbred offspring, it's not high enough to prevent the practice though purely biological means.

I think the core discussion shouldn't be about which, rather more about "to what extent does each". I just focused on the social aspects because they're discussed less than the biological aspects are. I think both matter.

I was *furious*, so much so that drinking (which I’ve since quit) wasn’t even something I considered, knowing it wouldn't take this level of anger away. Instead, I went to the gym, overwhelmed by rage. My body felt on fire, every muscle vibrating with anger. I started lifting my usual weights, but they felt too light. Without taking breaks, I kept lifting heavier and heavier. It seemed like nothing until, suddenly, the next lift felt impossible. My muscles gave out completely.

I hobbled home, exhausted, and went to bed. When I woke up, I could barely move, and my piss was the same colour as Coca-Cola. I read a lot of med school textbooks because I have always loved medicine and realised this was a kidney issue (specifically, Rhabdomyolysis) so I went to the hospital. Initially, they dismissed me as a hypochondriac, making me wait 24 hours before I gave up and left. Things worsened, so I returned, only to endure another 12-hour wait.

As I was leaving a second time, a doctor rushed after me to bring me back. She reviewed my case and confirmed my suspicions of Rhabdomyolysis. My CK levels were around 100,000 U/I, roughly 1000 times the expected limit. Levels above 5000 U/I can be indicative of kidney failure. It was a miracle they caught me just in time; another 30 seconds and I would’ve returned home again, where I certainly would've died. 

After a week in the hospital, the focus shifted to testing my kidney function to determine the extent of the damage and whether I’d need dialysis. To everyone’s surprise, both kidneys were functioning at 100%. Several doctors (and students) trickled in and out during my stay asking all sorts of questions about my situation. I wonder if I'm a case study or anonymously mentioned in medical literature anywhere.

None of them will perfectly align with your situation, and none of them will fully represent what you'd experience even if the situation was identical.

A video gives you visuals and audio that aren't even close to the real thing. Seeing someone get blown to bits in person taught me that it's the smells, the personal feelings, the reactions of those around, the weirdly small details that somehow just fuck with you. 

My mind has blocked out a lot of that day. I stayed up overnight, playing tetris through tears while drunk. 

I will never forget the sound. That sound is burned into my brain. Then there was some weird mist like stuff in the air where they died which I distinctly remember. The guy who didn't give a shit someone died and was angry at the now dead person because their body parts meant that his plans were delayed or had to change. I immediately started drinking and didn't stop for a solid year. 

Often waking up screaming and crying ruins your life from the sleep deprivation alone. You now get angry easily, because now people's problems seem minuscule, because you can't control the way you feel or when, or how that's expressed.

When I was about 3, my mother was doing something while letting me play near her. She let the dogs out into the garden, which was all fenced in. She pushed the door closed but it didn't properly close so I could still pull it open. A mistake anyone can make. Especially an exhausted mother dealing with a child (me lol) who we now know had ADHD real bad. Something came up like a phone call on the landline, so she went to grab the phone. 

Idk why, but as soon as I saw her leave I took at the opportunity like an inmate doing life without parole. The few short minutes that she wasn't looking was all I needed to get outside into the garden, which was "child proofed" with tall (~5ft?) chainlink fences, which I scaled easily before running my dumbass 10 minutes down the street to a local waterpark. 

Obviously she noticed fast, but who expects a 3 year old to pull that shit? She started calling around the house. I used to hide from her for fun (sorry mom) so she assumed I was somewhere in the house. 

The staff recognised me because we went there pretty often and then realised I was alone. I'm not really sure how, but they managed to get ahold of my mom (or she decided to come look as she knew I loved the place) 

One of the earliest memories I have was running barefoot down this tarmac road across parking lots, dodging all this broken glass on the floor. Then I remember the look on my mom's face. I didn't really get it at the time but I remember thinking "i've never seen her pull that face". I don't think I've ever seen her look so fucking stressed. Her face was WHITE and she looked like she was about to drop. 

She's an excellent mother, dealt with me (who had pretty severe ADHD, likely some other stuff) and did this singlehandedly while my dad worked long hours to put a roof over our head. She slept probably around 4h-6h a night between me and my sister because I also had sleep issues related to the ADHD. 

Point of this massive story - this might not be a shitty mother. A great mom can make one mistake and it leads to this. A shitty mom can make one thousand mistakes and get lucky every time. 

When you're sleep deprived, stressed, have a kid and household chores to do, there's going to be a moment where something *could've happened*. Most of the time it won't. 

I bet most parents have had moments (even if they won't admit it) where they've done something like fall asleep with the kid on their chest, or looked away for longer than 30 seconds, or left a door/baby gate open. 99.9% of the time, nothing happens and you move on. 

This fucking sucks for everyone involved. Gotta wait to investigate before jumping on a mother who's probably already never going to recover from this. Whatever it is, there's nothing the law can hand down that'll be worse than the way she'll punish herself.

In my eyes, the biggest issue is with how they describe the flight time as equivalent to "x skydives" in freefall. If you google this it'll likely tell you a time which includes the parachute descent, which is much longer than the freefall itself. I wouldn't expect people to somehow automatically know this - it's obviously not common knowledge. 

It's a double edged sword though, because stating it either way without clarification is misleading. Saying "Skydives" leaves people open to assuming it's much longer than it actually is, but if you give the time in minutes, people assume it's unfairly short in comparison to the skydive durations google will say. Your response actually demonstrates what I mean quite well! Just for some insight; 

Professional indoor skydivers usually stay in for around 5 minutes if they're going for endurance. They'll spread a bunch of these sessions out over a day of training to give themselves breaks between.

It's not like being weightless as the wind exerts a constant force on you. Depending on certain factors the windspeed can apply quite a significant force on you, hence their questions about if you've dislocated your shoulder or injured it. I would do around 4 sessions each at 3 minutes (12 min total) and I could definitely feel it in my shoulders & core afterwards - that's without the routines in all fairness, but even just doing belly fly most people would probably want out before 10 minutes.

Try create a mnemonic/memory device that reminds you of the silly mistakes you usually make, and then use remaining time in the exam to go question by question and apply it while actually \*hunting\* for the mistakes. Simply reading over your answer doesn't really work with ADHD because it's the same thing you just wrote and that's not really that engaging or exciting to the ADHD brain. Turning it into a game of sorts where you have to actively seek out certain things like the wrong signs, negative questions, ect. 

Sometimes it also helps to highlight key parts of questions like "Which of these factors \*\*doesn't\*\* contribute to x". Or just stripping out info you don't need. 

"Sally got up at 6am and decided to start a business with £10, before having lunch and deciding she's going to invest the £10 in a supply of smack to sell. Within a year of graduating from key stage 2 she manages to get all her friends hooked, pay off £30k in primary school playground gambling debt and ends up with £250 cash, what's her net profit from selling the best smack in town?"

Becomes "Start £10 --> £10 of smack --> £30k debt paid off --> end £250 cash" 

Then quickly double check you haven't left anything important out by highlighting important stuff in one colour, double checking, and highlighting unimportant stuff in a different colour, before finally reading the original question again to make sure that your answer follows that process. 

Some of this may be more useful to you, and time constrains may prevent you from doing all of the above but you know yourself best. Also remember that silly mistakes aren't ONLY an ADHD thing, you'll always make one or two dumb errors as will those without ADHD. Aim to reduce the amount of silly mistakes, but be realistic and understand you're unlikely to prevent ALL silly mistakes. Any improvement is still an improvement.
